property_summary: For any callee that reverts when receiving Ether, the reference contract's withdrawAll forwards the balance via its internal withdraw call (which uses transfer to msg.sender) only after the internal call path preserves ownership semantics; the mutated version directly transfer()s to msg.sender and thus will behave differently when withdrawAll is invoked by a contract that causes the internal call path to attempt sending to a different target — specifically, if withdrawAll's internal withdraw call would send to owner via payable(msg.sender) but the mutation changes recipient semantics when external reversion occurs, the mutant can fail to preserve that the contract's balance becomes zero after withdrawAll in some adversarial cases.

For any caller that is the owner and any contract recipient that may revert on receiving Ether, calling withdrawAll always results in the contract balance becoming zero in the reference (because it routes through internal withdraw call) while the mutant that replaces the internal call with a direct transfer to msg.sender can revert or fail to zero the balance for some adversarial recipient contract.

For any owner and any recipient contract that can revert on receiving Ether, calling withdrawAll always succeeds and leaves C's balance zero in the reference (which uses its internal withdraw call), whereas the mutant that directly transfer()s to msg.sender can cause the call to revert or leave funds in C when the recipient's receive/fallback reverts.

For any owner and any recipient contract that may revert when receiving Ether, calling withdrawAll from the owner always results in C's balance being zero (reference): the mutant that replaces the internal call with a direct transfer can leave C's balance non-zero for some adversarial recipient, so the property is violated.

For any owner and any recipient helper contract that refuses plain transfer (reverts on receive), calling withdrawAll via the reference C always results in the contract balance becoming zero (the internal withdraw call path succeeds or at least clears balance), but the mutant that replaces the internal call with a direct transfer can leave C's balance non-zero for some fuzzed deposit amount and adversarial recipient, so withdrawAll may not clear the balance.

For any caller who is the owner and any positive contract balance, calling withdrawAll always reduces the contract balance (sends the full balance to the owner); the mutant calling withdraw(0) can leave the contract balance unchanged for some positive balances, violating this rule.

For any caller who is the owner and any positive contract balance, calling withdrawAll always reduces address(c).balance (sends out the full balance); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave the contract balance unchanged for some positive balances, violating this rule.

If the owner calls withdrawAll after the contract has a positive balance, the reference C will transfer the entire contract balance to the owner (reducing address(c).balance), whereas the mutant that calls withdraw(0) may leave the contract balance unchanged; therefore for any positive funding amount and owner caller, withdrawAll must reduce address(c).balance (i.e., make the call succeed and contract balance decrease).

If the contract has a positive balance and the owner calls withdrawAll, then after the call the contract's balance becomes zero (reference transfers full balance; mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave balance > 0).

If the owner calls withdrawAll after the contract has a positive balance, then the owner's balance must increase by exactly the previous contract balance (i.e., withdrawAll forwards all contract funds to the owner); the mutant calling withdraw(0) violates this for some positive balances because the owner receives nothing.

For any caller and any balance, only the contract creator (owner) can successfully call withdrawAll and thus reduce the contract balance; the mutant inverts onlyOwner so a non-owner can withdraw and the original owner cannot, breaking this rule for some inputs.

For every caller and balance, the original contract guarantees that the deployer (owner) can successfully call withdrawAll (so withdrawAll does not revert when called by owner), while the mutant inverts onlyOwner and will cause withdrawAll to revert for the owner for some inputs (owner vs non-owner), so the property is: withdrawAll called by the original owner always succeeds.

For any caller address and any ether balance in the contract, the deployer (owner) can always successfully call withdrawAll (it does not revert) and thus can cause the contract balance to be forwarded; the mutant inverts onlyOwner so there exist inputs where the deployer cannot call withdrawAll (it reverts).

For every caller address and contract balance, calling withdrawAll from the deployer (owner) succeeds and transfers the contract balance out (so address(c).balance becomes zero); the mutant inverts onlyOwner so there exist inputs where the deployer cannot withdraw and address(c).balance remains non-zero.

For any arbitrary caller address and any nonzero contract balance funded by that caller, only the deployer (owner) is permitted to successfully call withdraw(uint) to transfer an arbitrary amount out; the mutant inverts onlyOwner and thus allows a non-owner to succeed for some inputs (a non-owner caller can withdraw while the owner cannot).

For every caller and amount, only the contract owner can successfully withdraw the contract balance via withdrawAll (i.e., withdrawAll calls invoked by non-owner must not reduce address(c).balance); the mutant removing the onlyOwner guard allows some non-owner callers to withdraw and thus change address(c).balance.

For every caller and any ether deposit, only the contract owner can successfully withdraw the contract's balance via withdrawAll; the mutant removing the onlyOwner modifier allows some non-owner caller to successfully withdraw and thus reduce address(c).balance.

For every caller who is not the owner, calling withdrawAll must either revert or leave the contract balance unchanged; the mutant (which removes onlyOwner) allows some non-owner caller to successfully drain the contract balance, violating this rule.

For any caller and any deposited amount, if the caller is not the contract owner then calling withdrawAll does not transfer the contract's balance to that caller (i.e., address(c).balance remains unchanged); the mutant removing onlyOwner allows a non-owner caller to drain the balance, violating this rule.

For every depositor and any deposit amount, if withdrawAll is invoked by the original contract owner then the call succeeds and drains the contract balance to the owner; the mutant (removing onlyOwner) allows some non-owner caller to successfully obtain the contract balance instead, so there exists a caller and deposit amount where a non-owner invocation of withdrawAll transfers the balance away (address(c).balance decreases) — we assert the owner-only successful drain property using a try/catch and balance checks.

For any caller who is the owner, calling withdraw(x) always reduces the contract balance by x and results in address(c).balance decreased by x (i.e., funds are sent to the caller); the mutant that sends funds to the stored owner instead can leave the contract balance unchanged for calls made by a different msg.sender owner-prank scenario and thus violates this property for some inputs.

For any caller who is the contract owner and any withdraw amount <= address(c).balance, calling withdraw(amount) always reduces address(c).balance by that amount (reference C sends funds to the caller); the mutant that sends funds to the stored owner can leave address(c).balance unchanged when the caller is owner but not the stored owner, so the rule is violated for some inputs.

For any caller A (fuzzed) who is the owner at call time and any value v (fuzzed) that is <= contract balance, after A calls withdraw(v) the contract's balance decreases by v (reference sends funds to msg.sender; mutant that sends to stored owner can leave balance unchanged when msg.sender != owner), so address(c).balance_post == address(c).balance_pre - v holds for all admissible inputs — which the mutant violates for some inputs.

For any caller A (fuzzed) who is NOT the stored owner and any value v ≤ contract balance, when A (as owner via vm.prank) calls withdraw(v) the reference contract sends v out of the contract (reducing address(c).balance by v), but the mutant that transfers to stored owner can leave the contract balance unchanged when msg.sender != owner, so the invariant address(c).balance_post == address(c).balance_pre - v holds for all admissible inputs in the reference and is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

For any caller A who is the contract owner at call time and any withdraw amount v ≤ contract balance, after A calls withdraw(v) the contract's balance decreases by v (the reference sends funds to msg.sender); the mutant that sends to stored owner can violate this when msg.sender != owner because funds are sent elsewhere.

For any target that reverts during a low-level call, the reference contract's sendMoney call does not revert (it swallows the failure because it ignores the return), whereas the mutant that assigns the returned success into a variable but does not use it still should not revert in Solidity — however the practical difference is that assigning the returned values changes compilation behavior so that when the callee reverts the mutant's external call will propagate the revert (causing sendMoney to revert) — hence the reference never reverts for any fuzzed value and target, but the mutant can revert for some targets that revert.

For any callee address and value, calling sendMoney never reverts (reference swallows low-level call failures by ignoring return), but the mutant that captures the call's (success, data) can make sendMoney revert when the callee reverts.

For any target contract and any value/data, C.sendMoney never reverts (it always returns successfully); the mutant can revert when the callee reverts, so there exist inputs (a reverting callee and suitable value) that make the mutant revert while the reference does not.

For every target address and calldata/value, the reference C.sendMoney never reverts (it swallows failing low-level calls); the mutant that assigns the (bool, bytes) return can propagate a callee revert, so there exist inputs (a reverting callee and nonzero value) that make the mutant revert while the reference still succeeds.

For any target contract and any value/calldata, the reference C.sendMoney never reverts (it always returns successfully because it ignores the low-level call return), whereas the mutant that captures the low-level call return values can allow a callee revert to propagate and thus may cause sendMoney to revert for some adversarial callee and input.

For any caller and any target/value/data, only the contract owner can cause the contract to send ether via sendMoney; the mutant (removing onlyOwner) allows a non-owner caller to force the contract to send value (changing address(c).balance) for some fuzzed inputs.

For every caller, calling sendMoney on the reference C does not change the contract balance unless the caller is the owner (onlyOwner); the mutant removes the guard so some non-owner caller can cause address(c).balance to decrease for some fuzzed inputs.

For all callers and inputs, only the owner can make C send ether out (so address(c).balance never decreases when called by a non-owner); the mutant removes onlyOwner from sendMoney so there exist non-owner calls and parameters that reduce address(c).balance, violating this rule.

For every caller and call parameters, calling sendMoney on the reference C will NOT succeed (i.e., will revert or be disallowed) when the caller is not the owner (only the owner can invoke sendMoney successfully); the mutant removes the onlyOwner guard so there exist non-owner callers for which sendMoney succeeds and thus this property is violated.

For every caller and inputs, calls to sendMoney on the reference contract C revert (are disallowed) when the caller is not the owner; the mutant removes onlyOwner so there exist a non-owner and parameters for which sendMoney succeeds, violating this rule.
